message:
QUESTION:
How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?

DATA:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [method] Ignores regression to the mean. The sites were selected because their 2020-2022 counts were the highest, so that period is likely inflated by chance, and counts would be expected to fall even without cameras. CORRECTION: The before period overstates the true underlying rate. An RTM adjustment (e.g. an empirical-Bayes estimate using longer histories or comparable sites) is needed, and the 27% figure is an upper bound.
F2. [omission] Ignores the 15% fall in traffic at the sites after the bypass opened, which would reduce collisions on its own. CORRECTION: Expected without cameras, allowing for trend and traffic: 52 × 0.90 × 0.85 = 39.8 a year, so about 6 prevented a year (roughly a 15% relative reduction), before any RTM adjustment.
F3. [misreport] The surveys show mean speed fell from 34 to 31 mph, still above the 30 mph limit. CORRECTION: A 3 mph fall in mean speed; speeds remain slightly above the limit.
F4. [inference] Generalises from 12 km of the highest-collision arterial roads to 900 km of mostly low-collision residential streets, with a selection-inflated effect estimate. CORRECTION: No city-wide estimate is supported. The effect on typical roads, which have low counts, would be much smaller in absolute terms and is unknown in relative terms.

EXTENSIONS:
- Request each site's collision counts for earlier years (e.g. 2015-2019) to estimate the regression-to-the-mean component directly.
- Split the 10 sites into the 6 affected by the bypass and the 4 not affected; the 4 unaffected sites give a cleaner (if small) estimate of the camera effect.
- Look at severity (killed or seriously injured vs slight), since speed reductions are expected to reduce severity more than frequency; even a modest 3 mph fall in mean speed may matter there.

FINAL VERSION:
# Average-Speed Cameras: Three-Year Evaluation

## Summary

Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites fell by 35%, from 156 to 102. Collisions on the rest of the city's roads fell by 10% over the same period. Allowing for that background trend gives a relative reduction of about **27%**. This probably overstates what the cameras achieved, for two reasons:

- **The sites were chosen for their unusually high 2020–2022 counts.** Part of the later fall would have happened anyway (regression to the mean).
- **A bypass opened in March 2023 and cut traffic at the sites by 15%.** Traffic on the comparison roads did not change.

Allowing for the bypass under typical assumptions gives a camera effect of about **15–21%**. The effect could be below 15% if the bypass mainly removed heavy through-traffic.

The speed data give an independent estimate. Mean speeds fell from 34 to 31 mph. Speed–collision models translate that into roughly a **9–17%** reduction in injury collisions, depending on the model.

Both estimates still include an unknown amount of regression to the mean, and both are statistically uncertain. Once the bypass is allowed for in any way, the 95% intervals include no effect, and those intervals are probably too narrow.

**Conclusion:** the cameras probably reduced injury collisions modestly. The reduction is perhaps somewhere around 10–20% before allowing for regression to the mean, which would lower it further. The effect is not statistically established.

**City-wide rollout:** these results do not support any forecast for a city-wide rollout. A figure of about 290 collisions prevented a year comes from applying 27% to all other roads, and it should not be used.

## Background

Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. This note compares injury collisions over the three full years before installation (2020–2022) with the three full years after (2023–2025). It covers the 10 sites and all other city roads.

All 10 sites are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, around 1.3% of its length. They have far more collisions per km than the rest of the network:

- **Camera sites (before):** about 4.3 injury collisions per km per year (52 a year over 12 km).
- **All other roads:** about 1.35 per km per year (1,200 a year over 888 km).

## Raw change

| | 2020–2022 | 2023–2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera sites | 156 (52/yr) | 102 (34/yr) | −35% |
| All other roads | 3,600 (1,200/yr) | 3,240 (1,080/yr) | −10% |

## Allowing for the background trend

The after-to-before ratio is 0.654 at the sites and 0.900 on other roads. Dividing one by the other gives 0.727, a relative reduction of about 27%.

Put another way, the 10% background fall would have taken the sites from 52 collisions a year to an expected 46.8. The observed figure was 34, a gap of about 13 a year.

Four problems mean the true camera effect is smaller, and less certain, than this 27% suggests.

### 1. Regression to the mean

The sites were chosen because they had the city's highest injury-collision counts in 2020–2022. Any site's count reflects its underlying risk plus chance. Sites selected for high counts will tend to have been unlucky in that period, so their counts would be expected to fall afterwards even with no intervention.

The 2020–2022 baseline is therefore biased upwards. The size of this bias cannot be estimated from the data available. Evaluations of speed-camera schemes have often found it to be a substantial share of the apparent effect.

Estimating it needs either:

- collision counts at the sites for earlier years (for example 2015–2019), or
- an empirical Bayes analysis using similar arterial roads without cameras.

### 2. The bypass reduced traffic at the sites

The bypass diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Average traffic at the sites fell by 15%. Traffic on the comparison roads was broadly unchanged, so the trend adjustment does not capture this fall.

The 15% is an average across all 10 sites. Suppose the fall was concentrated at the 6 affected sites, with little change at the other 4, and volumes are similar across sites. Then traffic at those 6 fell by roughly 25%. The 6 sites therefore probably look quite different from the other 4, which is why a site-by-site analysis is worthwhile.

How much of the collision fall the bypass explains depends on how collisions respond to traffic volume:

| How collisions respond to traffic | Traffic factor | Expected without cameras (/yr) | Camera ratio | Camera effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Not at all (elasticity 0) | 1.00 | 46.8 | 0.727 | ~27% |
| Collisions ∝ traffic^0.5 | 0.922 | 43.1 | 0.789 | ~21% |
| Proportionally (elasticity 1) | 0.85 | 39.8 | 0.855 | ~15% |

The full span is 15–27%. The top of that span assumes that removing 15% of traffic had no effect on collisions, which is implausible. Road-safety models usually find that collisions rise with traffic, but less than proportionally. That makes **15–21%** the more realistic range.

The adjustment could also be too small. If the bypass mainly removed heavy through-traffic, its safety benefit could exceed what the volume change alone implies, and the camera effect would be below 15%.

### 3. The COVID-19 baseline

The 2020–2022 baseline includes pandemic years with unusual traffic volumes and speeds. These conditions may have affected arterial roads differently from mostly residential streets. This casts further doubt on "all other roads" as a comparison group. The direction of the resulting bias is unclear.

### 4. Small numbers and statistical uncertainty

The counts at the sites are small. Treating them as Poisson gives approximate 95% intervals:

| Estimate | Ratio | Approx. 95% interval | Includes no effect? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trend-adjusted only | 0.727 | 0.56–0.94 | No |
| √traffic adjustment | 0.789 | 0.61–1.02 | Yes |
| Proportional traffic adjustment | 0.855 | 0.66–1.10 | Yes |

These intervals understate the true uncertainty in three ways:

- They ignore overdispersion, meaning the extra variation between sites and years.
- They treat the traffic adjustment as known exactly.
- They make no allowance for regression to the mean.

Once the bypass is allowed for in any way, the data are consistent with no camera effect.

## Speeds

Speed surveys at the sites show mean speeds falling from 34 mph to 31 mph. That is a 3 mph reduction, and the mean is still slightly above the 30 mph limit. This is the clearest direct evidence that the cameras changed driver behaviour.

The speed change also gives a rough independent estimate of the collision effect. Power Model relationships link injury collisions to mean speed raised to an exponent:

- Nilsson's general exponent for injury collisions is 2.
- Later re-estimates (Elvik) found lower exponents on urban roads, roughly 1.0–1.5.

| Exponent | (31/34)^exponent | Implied reduction |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 0.912 | ~9% |
| 1.5 | 0.871 | ~13% |
| 2.0 | 0.831 | ~17% |

The likely urban exponents point to roughly 9–13%, and the general exponent gives 17%. The speed evidence therefore supports a reduction somewhere around 10–17%. That broadly agrees with the collision-based estimates, overlapping the lower end of the bypass-adjusted 15–21% range.

The speed evidence has two advantages:

- It does not depend on the choice of comparison roads.
- It is much less affected by regression to the mean, because the sites were selected on collisions rather than on speeds.

It also has three limitations:

- **Selection is not wholly irrelevant.** Sites with unusually high collision counts may also have had unusually high speeds at the time.
- **Survey timing matters.** The "before" survey may have been taken during 2020–21. If so, pandemic-era empty roads probably inflated the baseline speed, which would overstate the fall. The survey dates and number of surveys should be reported alongside these figures.
- **The bypass's effect on speeds could go either way.** Lighter traffic usually allows higher free-flow speeds, which would mean the cameras' true speed effect is larger than the observed 3 mph. A change in traffic mix could work the other way.

## City-wide rollout

The evaluation does not support an estimate of what a city-wide rollout would achieve. Applying a 27% reduction to all 1,080 collisions a year on other roads would give about 290 a year, but that calculation is not valid, for three reasons:

- **The 27% is overstated** because of the bypass and regression to the mean. Once these are allowed for, the effect is not statistically established even at the original sites.
- **The effect was measured on 12 km of high-collision arterial roads.** Most of the remaining 888 km is residential streets with low collision counts and different traffic conditions. Average-speed cameras are designed for corridors and rarely suit residential streets. There is no basis for assuming the same percentage effect there.
- **The benefit per camera falls steeply on lower-risk roads.** There are few collisions per km to prevent, while installation and running costs stay similar.

Any extension should be framed as targeted deployment on other high-risk arterial corridors, not as a city-wide programme.

## Recommendations

1. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
2. **Re-analyse the existing sites before deciding on any extension.** Specifically:
   - Obtain pre-2020 collision data for the 10 sites, or carry out an empirical Bayes analysis, to estimate regression to the mean. Pre-2020 data would also give a baseline unaffected by COVID-19.
   - Analyse the 6 bypass-affected sites and the 4 unaffected sites separately, using site-level traffic counts.
   - Use comparison sites of the same road type (arterials), not all other roads.
   - Use models that allow for overdispersion when estimating uncertainty.
   - Report speed-survey dates and sample sizes, and repeat the speed–collision cross-check at the 4 unaffected sites.
   - Examine collision severity as well as counts.
3. **If the corrected effect is still worthwhile, pilot cameras on a small number of further high-risk arterial corridors.** Design the pilot so it can be evaluated properly, with comparable control corridors. Its baselines should not use the same years that were used to select the sites.
4. **Continue annual monitoring** of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites.

## Costs and publication

Average-speed camera systems carry installation, maintenance and enforcement costs. A business case for any extension should set these against a corrected estimate of collisions prevented, valued by severity. The evaluation should be published, including its limitations, so residents can see the results.

---

**Covering note (send separately; not part of the report)**

Changes from the earlier draft. The draft itself was not available to me, so please check each item against it before circulating:

- **Speed figure corrected.** The data show the mean speed falling to 31 mph, not 26 mph. That is still above the 30 mph limit, not "well below" it.
- **Baseline.** The draft called the 2020–2022 baseline "fair". It is biased upwards by regression to the mean and also covers the COVID-19 period.
- **Bypass adjustment added.** It reduces the estimated effect to about 15–21% under typical assumptions, and possibly lower.
- **Speed cross-check added**, using a range of exponents. It gives about 9–17%.
- **Uncertainty quantified.** Once the bypass is allowed for, the intervals include no effect, and they are probably too narrow.
- **City-wide claim removed.** The draft's figure of about 290 a year is consistent with 1,080 × 0.27 ≈ 292, but that calculation is not valid.
- **Recommendation changed** from city-wide funding to a corrected analysis plus a targeted, properly evaluated pilot.
- **Correct arithmetic kept.** The draft's figures of 35%, 10%, 0.727, and 46.8 versus 34 are unchanged.
